title: Checkpoint: Music Around the World
objective: After this level you can compare musical traditions from India, Indonesia, Africa, the Middle East and the Americas.
summary: Music turns in cycles: Indian tala, the Javanese gongan, the Ewe bell phrase. A West African bell pattern crossed the Atlantic with enslaved Africans; in Cuba it is son clave.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: around the world, music comes back around.
cards.body: Look back across this chapter and a pattern jumps out. Indian tala, Javanese gamelan and Ewe drumming all build music on a cycle that repeats, and each tradition marks the turn in its own way. One of those cycles even crossed an ocean.

cards.headline: Three ways to mark a cycle

items.label: India: tala
points: Resolves on sam, the first beat

items.label: Java: gamelan
points: The great gong ageng marks each end

items.label: Ghana: Ewe Agbadza
points: The gankogui bell repeats one phrase

cards.headline: The bell pattern that crossed the Atlantic
cards.body: A Smithsonian Folkways lesson teaches that West African polyrhythmic traditions followed Africans to the Caribbean as a result of the transatlantic slave trade. You can hear the link. Folkways points to 'Gome,' from the album Folk Music of Ghana: its pattern would be called son clave if it were played in Afro-Cuban music. That's the clave from Level 58, the foundation of Afro-Cuban music and the pulse under salsa.

cards.headline: Melody's cousins: raga and maqam
cards.body: Cycles organize time; modes organize melody. Britannica calls the maqam roughly related to the Indian raga. Both start from a set of notes, both come with characteristic motifs, and both invite improvisation inside the rules: a raga performer uses only the raga's notes, and a taqsim wanders from its home maqam and comes back. Across the world, a mode is a way of moving, not just a list of notes.

mascot.line: Ten levels, one lesson: every tradition keeps its own time and its own notes.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: How the world's traditions differ in scales, time cycles and instruments, and why each has its own rules.
Why a raga or a maqam is more than a scale: a set of notes plus motifs and rules for improvising.
How a first beat, a great gong or a repeating bell pattern keeps musicians together through a cycle.
How a West African bell pattern crossed the Atlantic to become the clave under Afro-Cuban music.

options.label: Gongan cycle
options.rationale: A gongan is a Javanese gamelan cycle.

questions.prompt: How did West African rhythmic traditions reach Afro-Cuban music, as this chapter tells it?

options.label: Cuban musicians studied them from printed scores in European libraries
options.rationale: The traditions traveled with people, not through scores.

options.label: They arrived through shortwave radio broadcasts in the 1970s
options.rationale: The link is far older than radio.

options.label: They developed separately, and the patterns match by pure coincidence
options.rationale: Folkways traces a direct line across the Atlantic.

options.label: They followed Africans to the Caribbean through the transatlantic slave trade

questions.explanation: Smithsonian Folkways teaches that West African polyrhythmic traditions followed enslaved Africans to the Caribbean.

questions.prompt: From Level 52's Indian classical music: how many beats make one cycle of the Hindustani tala tintal?

options.rationale: Twelve is flamenco's compas, not tintal.

questions.explanation: Tintal has 16 beats in four groups of four.

questions.prompt: From Level 53's gamelan: how do the slendro and pelog tunings differ?

options.label: Slendro: five near-equal steps; pelog: seven pitches, narrow and wide steps
Slendro is used only in Bali; pelog only in India
Pelog follows the piano's 12 semitones; slendro has 24 steps
options.rationale: Pelog has seven pitches per octave and slendro five.

options.label: They are one tuning, with different names in each village
options.rationale: Their note counts and step sizes differ.

questions.explanation: Slendro has five nearly equal notes per octave; pelog has seven with clearly narrow and wide steps.

questions.prompt: From Level 55: in a taqsim improvisation, where does the performer end up?

Back in the home maqam where it started
